reconcile.connective: Commentators read the two claims as different domains: Jewish law found Jesus worthy of death, but Rome alone held the power to execute.

discrepancy.connective: Daniel G. Taylor's BibViz Project lists the two verses as a stand-alone contradiction, presenting 'not lawful' against 'he ought to die' without resolution.

excerpts.excerpt_text: They were conscious they had no case of which Pilate could take cognizance, and therefore insinuate that they had already found Him worthy of death by their own law; but not having the power, under the Roman government, to carry their sentence into execution, they had come merely for his sanction.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the two claims: found worthy of death under their own law, yet lacking power to carry out execution under Rome.

excerpts.excerpt_text: They might have judged Jesus according to their law, as Pilate bade them do; but they could only excommunicate or scourge him. They might have voted him worthy of death; but they could not put him to death, if any thing of a secular nature were charged against him.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explains 'not lawful' (18:31) as a lack of executive power to execute, even though their own law could pronounce him worthy of death (matching 19:7).

excerpts.excerpt_text: For judgments of life and death were taken from them forty years before the destruction of the temple.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gives the historical reason the Jewish authorities lacked capital jurisdiction, supporting the harmonization of the 'not lawful' statement with 19:7's verdict.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing under the heading 'Christ's execution -- Lawful, Unlawful' (John 19:7 vs. John 18:31), p. 220, resolving it as Mosaic verdict versus Roman restriction on carrying out execution.
